id: ch4-vm-p2 / ch4-vm-p7 / ch4-vm-p8 / fig-4-8 vs chBridge-mmu-p2 / chBridge-mmu-p5 / fig-br-4
quote: Walking all four levels on every access would turn each memory access into five
problem: ch4-vm-p1 says the Bridge already showed the MMU and TLB, and that this section covers the kernel's side. Then p2 defines the MMU again in bold. p4 and p5 redo the Bridge's 512 GB flat-table arithmetic and the split into four levels of 512 entries. p7 and p8 retell chBridge-mmu-p5 almost sentence for sentence: the 5x cost, the >99% hit rate, the translations dropped on a switch unless tagged. Fig 4.8 redraws Fig BR.4's walk down from CR3. Two details also disagree: p2 says the MMU is 'built into the CPU' where the Bridge says it sits 'between the CPU and the RAM', and the units change from KiB/GiB to KB/GB.
fix: Keep p1 and turn p2 to p8 into a recall. p2: "Every load and store uses a virtual address, which the MMU of Fig BR.4 translates through the page table the kernel builds and keeps current." Keep Fig 4.8 as the one new picture (a real address split into its four indices) and cut p4 and p5 to the 2^36-pages count that Fig 4.8 needs. Replace p7 and p8 with: "A TLB hit (Fig BR.5) skips the walk. What the kernel has to manage is the switch: changing CR3 drops the old process's translations unless each entry carries an address-space tag (PCID on x86)."
reason: ch4-vm-p7 and p8 retell chBridge-mmu-p5 almost sentence for sentence (5x tax, >99% hit rate, CR3 switch drops translations unless tagged, PCID is already in Fig BR.5's strip). p2 re-bolds the MMU the Bridge defined. p4/p5 are NOT pure repetition: the 2^36 count, the 9-bit index split and 'a few megabytes of tables' are new and Fig 4.8 needs them, so keep those.
judge_fix: p2: "Every load and store uses a _virtual address_, which the MMU of Fig BR.4 translates to a _physical address_ through the *page table* the kernel builds and keeps current." Replace p7+p8 with one paragraph: "A TLB hit (Fig BR.5) skips the walk, so the cost the kernel has to manage is the miss. Each miss costs up to four extra memory reads, and a switch to another process drops the old translations unless each entry is tagged with its address space (PCID on x86), which is why processes still compete for the same few entries." Keep p3, p4, p5 and Fig 4.8 (units: see finding 22). Optionally drop 'as the Bridge showed' from p5 since p1 says it.

quote: so a NULL access always traps
problem: The section opens by saying that dereferencing a null pointer is undefined, so the standard requires nothing, 'not even a crash'. Fig 5.8's strip adds that Linux builds with -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks. The NULL subsection then presents a guaranteed crash, and Fig 5.9's strip says it 'always traps'. A careful reader will ask how undefined behaviour can always crash. The missing link: the trap happens only if the compiled code still contains the access. ch5-ub-p5 also says 'the very first page' where the strip says 'the lowest pages'.
fix: Strip: "Operating systems leave the lowest pages unmapped on purpose (Linux's mmap_min_addr), so a NULL access that reaches the processor traps." Add to the end of ch5-ub-p5: "That crash is the lucky case: because the dereference is undefined, the optimiser may assume the pointer was never NULL and delete a check that follows it, which is why Linux builds with -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks." In p5, say "the lowest pages".
reason: Section opens with 'no requirement at all, not even a crash', lists null dereference as UB, then the strip of Fig 5.9 says a NULL access 'always traps'. The missing link is real: the trap happens only if the access survives compilation. p5 also says 'the very first page' while the strip says 'the lowest pages' (mmap_min_addr covers many pages).
judge_fix: Fig 5.9 strip: "Operating systems leave the lowest pages unmapped on purpose (Linux's `mmap_min_addr`), so a NULL access that reaches the processor traps." Combine with finding 6 in p5 (see that fix), which ends: "That crash is the lucky outcome. Because the dereference is undefined, the optimiser may assume the pointer was never NULL and delete a NULL check that follows it, which is why Linux also builds with `-fno-delete-null-pointer-checks` (Fig 5.8)."

quote: a lock on every object slowed single-threaded code, which is most code, by 30–50%
problem: p2 says a lock on every object was what made earlier GIL removals too slow (30–50%). Fig 7.4's strip then says the successful PEP 703 build 'uses per-object locks'. The reader is not told why the same mechanism now costs 5–10%.
fix: p2: "Removing it has been tried many times, but earlier attempts made every reference-count update atomic and slowed single-threaded code, which is most code, by 30–50%. PEP 703, accepted in 2023, lets the thread that owns an object update its count without atomics (biased reference counting), which cuts the slowdown to about 5–10%." The strip can then keep "per-object locks and biased reference counting".
reason: Real tension. p2 blames 'a lock on every object' for the 30-50% slowdown, while Fig 7.4's strip says the successful PEP 703 build 'uses per-object locks'. I checked PEP 703: it does use per-object locks and biased reference counting, and reports about 5-6% single-thread overhead (matches the UNDER.md ledger line). Also note the 30-50% figure for earlier attempts is not in the UNDER.md ledger and PEP 703 gives no Gilectomy numbers, so the number should be sourced or softened.
judge_fix: p2: "Removing it has been tried many times, but earlier attempts made every reference-count update atomic or locked and slowed single-threaded code, which is most code, by a large margin. PEP 703, accepted in 2023, lets the thread that owns an object update its count without atomic instructions (biased reference counting), which has cut that slowdown to about 5–10%." If the author wants to keep '30–50%', add a source in the ledger first (not verifiable from PEP 703 itself). Fig 7.4 strip can stay as it is, since it already says 'per-object locks and biased reference counting'.

quote: a moved-from object is in a valid but unspecified state, and reading it is allowed but tells you nothing
problem: Two paragraphs earlier, p4 and Fig 6.8 show v1's pointers set to null, and the caption says 'v1 is left empty but still valid'. The glossary entry for move semantics also says 'valid but empty'. The closing strip then says a moved-from object is unspecified and reading it 'tells you nothing'. The reader cannot tell which applies to v1.
fix: "Use-after-move: apart from a few types such as the vector of Fig 6.8, which is left empty, a moved-from object is valid but unspecified, so reading it is allowed but tells you nothing you can rely on."
reason: Fig 6.8 caption says v1 is 'empty but still valid' and the glossary says a moved-from vector is empty; the closing strip says a moved-from object is unspecified and reading it 'tells you nothing'. A reader cannot tell which applies to v1. The finding's 'a few types' is slightly too narrow, so use softer wording.
judge_fix: "Use-after-move: in general a moved-from object is valid but unspecified, so reading it is allowed but gives you nothing to rely on (the vector of Fig 6.8 happens to be left empty, but most types promise less)."

id: ch4-scheduling-p4 (CFS row) / fig-4-4 (strip) / ch4 closer ¶1 vs ch13-indexes-p1
quote: O(log N) per scheduling decision via a red-black tree.
problem: Big-O notation appears three times in Chapter 4 (the table, Fig 4.4's strip and the closer) with no gloss and no glossary entry. The book first explains O(N) and O(log N) in ch13-indexes-p1, in Part IV.
fix: Table: "Each decision costs one step more each time the number of processes doubles (written O(log N)), thanks to a red-black tree." Fig 4.4 strip: "removing it and inserting a process each take one step more each time the tree doubles, so it stays quick with thousands runnable." Closer: "does this in a handful of steps even with thousands of processes".
reason: I grepped parts 1 and 2: the first Big-O notation in the book is the CFS table row, with no gloss and no glossary entry; it is next used in the Fig 4.4 strip and the chapter closer. The newcomer reader is first taught O(N)/O(log N) in Part IV. The informal 'stays quick even with thousands' in p5 helps, but the first use is the table.
judge_fix: Table CFS row, trade-off cell: "... Each decision takes one more step each time the number of processes doubles (written O(log N)), thanks to a red-black tree." Fig 4.4 strip and the closer may then keep 'O(log N)' because it is glossed once at first use; if the owner prefers, closer: "does this in a handful of steps even with thousands of processes".

quote: converts it into a signal called SIGSEGV ("segmentation violation"), which by default kills the process
problem: ch4-vm-p12 and Fig 4.9 already teach this path: an unmapped address such as NULL, a page fault, SIGSEGV, the program killed with 'segmentation fault'. ch4-ipc teaches signals. ch5-ub-p5 introduces SIGSEGV as if it were new ('a signal called') and retells the whole path. Fig 5.9's own strip admits it is Fig 4.9's invalid exit.
fix: Rewrite p5 as a recall: "NULL, the pointer value 0, points nowhere by convention, and the kernel leaves the lowest pages of every address space unmapped, so a NULL access takes the invalid exit of Fig 4.9: SIGSEGV, and the 'Segmentation fault (core dumped)' that has greeted C programmers for fifty years." Then add the undefined-behaviour point from the finding above.
reason: ch4-vm-p12 and Fig 4.9 already teach the NULL/unmapped address, page fault, SIGSEGV, 'segmentation fault' path, and Fig 5.9's own strip admits it is Fig 4.9's invalid exit. ch5-ub-p5 introduces SIGSEGV as 'a signal called' and retells it all. Recall is enough; Fig 5.9 keeps the end-to-end picture.
judge_fix: Rewrite ch5-ub-p5: "A pointer with the value `0` (or `NULL`, C's name for it) is conventionally \"the address that points nowhere.\" The kernel keeps the lowest pages of every address space unmapped, so a NULL access takes the invalid exit of Fig 4.9: a page fault, `SIGSEGV`, and the `Segmentation fault (core dumped)` message that has greeted C programmers for fifty years. That crash is the lucky outcome. Because the dereference is undefined, the optimiser may assume the pointer was never NULL and delete a NULL check that follows it, which is why Linux also builds with `-fno-delete-null-pointer-checks` (Fig 5.8)."

id: fig-5-3 (caption ch5-bell-labs-p8) / fig-5-2 (strip) / ch5-bell-labs-p5 vs ch5-portability-p7
quote: which is why C, unlike B, gave its pointers types
problem: The same story (B saw only words, the PDP-11 addressed bytes, so Ritchie added types) is told in ch5-portability-p7, again in Fig 5.2's 'Why C' strip bullet, again in ch5-bell-labs-p5, and again in Fig 5.3's caption and strip. The PDP-11 is also introduced twice (ch5-portability-p2 'shipped in 1970', ch5-bell-labs-p5 'sold from 1970 onwards').
fix: Tell it once, in ch5-portability-p7, and make Fig 5.3 its picture (add "(Fig 5.3)" after "had no direct way to reach one"). Cut Fig 5.2's "Why C" bullet. Shorten ch5-bell-labs-p5 to the machine itself: "The PDP-11 was a 16-bit minicomputer the size of a refrigerator, with eight registers, byte-addressable memory and a clean, regular instruction set. To a first approximation, C is a portable PDP-11 assembler." End Fig 5.3's caption at "by 1 and a pointer to an integer by 2".
reason: The B-saw-only-words / PDP-11-addresses-bytes / so-C-got-types story is told in ch5-portability-p7, Fig 5.2's 'Why C' bullet and Fig 5.3's caption, and the PDP-11's 1970 arrival is stated three times. But the proposed fix is wrong in one part: adding '(Fig 5.3)' in portability-p7 would point forward into a later section. Fig 5.3 belongs in bell-labs; keep its caption and the pointer-step sentence in bell-labs-p5, which is the figure's natural prose anchor.
judge_fix: Cut Fig 5.2's 'Why C' strip bullet (p7 tells it). In ch5-bell-labs-p5 drop the repeated date: "The PDP-11 was a 16-bit minicomputer: small (the size of a refrigerator, not a room), with eight general-purpose registers, byte-addressable memory and a clean, regular instruction set." Keep the rest of p5 (with finding 16's fix) and keep Fig 5.3's caption as is.

quote: A class compiles to a struct plus ordinary functions, its methods, at no extra cost.
problem: p5 gives Section 03's content in advance: a class is a struct plus functions at no cost, and a virtual method costs one hidden pointer and one call through a table. ch6-classes-p2 and p3 then explain both again in full. The zero-cost principle is also already stated in ch6-stroustrup-p2 and the chapter hero, and it has its own section (05).
fix: Cut ch6-stroustrup-p5 to: "What Stroustrup built was a deal: you may add abstraction without losing speed. Section 03 shows the deal in memory." Or delete it, since ch6-stroustrup-p2 already states the principle.
reason: ch6-stroustrup-p5 previews the content of Section 03 (class = struct + functions, virtual = hidden pointer + table call), which ch6-classes-p2/p3 then explain in full, and the zero-cost principle is already in stroustrup-p2. Trimming loses nothing.
judge_fix: ch6-stroustrup-p5: "What Stroustrup built was a deal: _you may add abstraction without losing speed_. Section 03 shows what that costs, in memory."

quote: so work that must respond quickly runs on time rather than merely fairly
problem: EEVDF is said to make urgent work 'run on time' (the strip says 'latency-sensitive work runs on time'). A few paragraphs later, general-purpose schedulers 'guarantee nothing about the worst case', and deadlines need a real-time kernel. A reader may conclude that Linux's default scheduler now meets deadlines.
fix: p5: "so work that must respond quickly gets the CPU sooner, rather than merely in turn." Strip: "so latency-sensitive work is picked sooner, though without the guarantee a real-time kernel gives."
reason: p5 and the Fig 4.4 strip say EEVDF makes urgent work 'run on time', while p12 says general-purpose schedulers guarantee nothing about the worst case and deadlines need a real-time kernel. EEVDF's deadline is a virtual one, not a wall-clock guarantee. Also p12 names only CFS although the default is now EEVDF.
judge_fix: p5 ending: "... gives every task an explicit virtual deadline, so work that must respond quickly is picked sooner, rather than merely in turn." Fig 4.4 strip: "... picks the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline, so latency-sensitive work is picked sooner, though without the guarantee a real-time kernel gives." p12: "General-purpose schedulers like CFS and EEVDF optimise for average performance ..."

id: ch6-classes h3 'Inheritance is layout' (no id) vs fig-6-4
quote: Inheritance is layout
problem: The subheading promises the layout of inheritance (ch6-classes-p1: 'a Circle object begins with a complete Shape'), but only Fig 6.4 sits under it, and Fig 6.4 shows dispatch through a vtable slot. There is no prose under the heading. An earlier pass flagged this and it is unchanged.
fix: Rename the heading "One call, many classes", or add one sentence under it: "A Circle object begins with a complete Shape, its vptr first, so code compiled for a Shape finds every field where it expects; Fig 6.4 shows what that buys."
reason: Verified in public/part-2.html (line 3395): the h3 'Inheritance is layout' is followed directly by Fig 6.4, which shows dispatch through a vtable slot, with no prose. ch6-classes-p1 promises 'a Circle object begins with a complete Shape' and nothing shows it. One sentence closes the gap.
judge_fix: Add under the heading: "A Circle object begins with everything a Shape has, its vptr first, so code compiled for a Shape finds each field where it expects it. Fig 6.4 shows what that buys: one call, three classes."

quote: one misbehaving program that never yields freezes the entire machine
problem: The Bridge already explained cooperative multitasking and the program that never yields and freezes the machine. ch4-scheduling-p2 explains it again as new. p3 credits the Bridge for the timer only. Later, ch7-gil-p2 refers to 'the Bridge's cooperative programs', so the book now has two first explanations.
fix: "The Bridge's cooperative kernel was real: Mac OS through version 9 and 16-bit Windows ran that way, light and simple, until one program that never yielded froze the machine."
reason: chBridge-timer-p1 already explains cooperative multitasking and the never-yielding program freezing the machine; ch4-scheduling-p2 restates it nearly verbatim as new, while p3 credits the Bridge only for the timer. The Mac OS 9 / 16-bit Windows examples are the new content and should stay.
judge_fix: ch4-scheduling-p2: "The earliest multi-tasking systems were _cooperative_, the model the Bridge described: each running program voluntarily yielded control back to the scheduler when it had nothing useful to do. Mac OS through version 9 worked this way, as did 16-bit Windows. It was simple and lightweight, until one program that never yielded froze the entire machine."

quote: C++11 is the pivot, adding move semantics, lambdas, auto and smart pointers
problem: The same four C++11 features are listed three times in one chapter: Fig 6.2's caption, ch6-modern-p1 and Fig 6.9's strip. In Section 02 the caption uses 'move semantics' and 'lambdas' before ch6-modern explains them.
fix: Fig 6.2 caption: "From Simula's classes to C++23: Stroustrup's C with Classes (1979) became C++, standardised in 1998. C++11 is the pivot (Section 06), and every standard since has added more while keeping almost all older code compiling." Fig 6.9 strip: keep only "C++20 (concepts, modules, ranges, coroutines) changed what 'modern C++' means a second time."
reason: The four C++11 features are listed in Fig 6.2's caption, ch6-modern-p1 and Fig 6.9's strip; the Fig 6.2 caption in Section 02 uses 'move semantics' and 'lambdas' before Section 06 explains them (the picture already says 'move, lambdas, auto').
judge_fix: Fig 6.2 caption: "From Simula's classes to C++23: Stroustrup's C with Classes (1979) became C++, standardised in 1998. C++11 is the pivot (Section 06), and every standard since has added more while keeping almost all older code compiling." Fig 6.9 strip first bullet: "C++20 (concepts, modules, ranges, coroutines) changed what 'modern C++' means a second time."

quote: 1 byte for a character, 2 for an integer (Fig 5.3)
problem: Stated as a general fact about C pointers, the int step is 2 here and 4 in the next section and in Fig 5.4. Fig 5.3 shows that the 2 is the PDP-11's, but the sentence does not say so.
fix: "steps by the size of what it points at: on the PDP-11, 1 byte for a character and 2 for an integer (Fig 5.3)."
reason: bell-labs-p5 states 'steps by the size of what it points at: 1 byte for a character, 2 for an integer' as a general fact about C pointers; Section 03 and Fig 5.4 then say 4 for int. The 2 is the PDP-11's.
judge_fix: "A C pointer, a variable that holds an address (Section 03 explains them), steps by the size of what it points at: on the PDP-11, 1 byte for a character and 2 for an integer (Fig 5.3)."

quote: served as the language's definition until the ANSI standard of 1989
problem: Fig 5.2's 'The book' bullet gives K&R's role and the 1989 ANSI date. ch5-bell-labs-p6 says the same a few lines later.
fix: Cut the "The book" bullet from Fig 5.2's strip. p6 tells it.
reason: Fig 5.2's 'The book' bullet says the same as ch5-bell-labs-p6 (K&R 1978, definition until ANSI 1989) a few lines later; it adds nothing.
judge_fix: Cut the 'The book' bullet from Fig 5.2's strip.

quote: Doug McIlroy's summary: write programs that do one thing well, and write them to work together.
problem: Fig 4.16's last bullet paraphrases the McIlroy pull-quote that comes straight after it. Fig 4.15's 'The lineage' bullet repeats ch4-ipc-p3 (McIlroy pressed for years, Thompson added pipes in 1973).
fix: Cut "The philosophy" bullet from Fig 4.16 (the pull-quote carries it) and "The lineage" bullet from Fig 4.15 (p3 carries it).
reason: Fig 4.16's 'The philosophy' bullet paraphrases the McIlroy pull-quote that follows immediately; Fig 4.15's 'The lineage' bullet repeats ch4-ipc-p3 almost word for word.
judge_fix: Cut 'The philosophy' from Fig 4.16's strip and 'The lineage' from Fig 4.15's strip.

quote: the table alone would need 512 GB per process
problem: The same quantities are written in binary units in the Bridge (4 KiB pages, 512 GiB flat table) and in decimal units in Chapter 4 (4 KB, 512 GB, 256 terabytes).
fix: Use one form. To match the Bridge: "4 KiB", "512 GiB", "256 TiB" in ch4-vm-p3 to p5 and the Fig 4.8 strip.
reason: The Bridge uses 4 KiB / 512 GiB (Pass 29 made pages '4 KiB' on purpose); ch4-vm-p3 to p5 and the Fig 4.8 strip restate the same quantities in decimal (4 KB, 512 GB, 256 terabytes). Same numbers on adjacent pages in two unit systems invites a doubt. Limited to the page-table arithmetic; the 64 KB pipe and other everyday sizes can stay decimal.
judge_fix: ch4-vm-p3 '4 KiB'; p4 '256 TiB', '4 KiB (2^12-byte) pages', '512 GiB per process'; p5 '4 KiB page', '256 TiB', '512 gibibytes' (or 'not 512 GiB'); Fig 4.8 strip '4 KiB' (three places) and Fig 4.8 drawn label if it says KB.

id: fig-4-2 (desc, caption ch4-anatomy-p9, strip) vs ch4-anatomy-p4 / ch4-fs

quote: Fred Brooks, The Mythical Man-Month (1975), applied the count to people
problem: The strip repeats p2's point that adding people to a late project makes it later, and renames 'Frederick Brooks' as 'Fred Brooks'.
fix: Strip bullet: "The source. Brooks counted channels between people: n people need n(n − 1)/2 of them."
reason: Fig 6.1's 'The source' bullet repeats ch6-complexity-p2's point (adding people to a late project makes it later) and says 'Fred Brooks' where the prose says 'Frederick Brooks'. The n(n-1)/2 link is the useful new part.
judge_fix: "*The source.* Brooks, in _The Mythical Man-Month_ (1975), counted channels between people: n people need n(n − 1)/2 of them."

quote: where arguments arrive (edi/esi, w0/w1, a0/a1)
problem: The figure draws 'a in rdi, b in rsi'. Its strip says the arguments arrive in edi/esi, with no note that these are the same registers' lower halves.
fix: "where arguments arrive (rdi/rsi, w0/w1, a0/a1)", or "(edi/esi, the 32-bit halves of rdi/rsi, ...)".
reason: The strip lists x86 arguments as edi/esi while the figure draws 'a in rdi, b in rsi' and the asm uses rdi/rsi. edi/esi are the 32-bit halves, which the strip does not say; a newcomer sees a mismatch.
judge_fix: "... where arguments arrive (`rdi`/`rsi`, `w0`/`w1`, `a0`/`a1`) and where the result goes back."

quote: By the late 1980s these languages ran most systems that mattered
problem: 'These languages' means C and C++. Section 02 says C++ 1.0 came only in 1985 and became dominant 'by 2000'.
fix: "By the late 1980s C ran most systems that mattered and C++ was spreading fast, and many programmers took this as the trade every language must make."
reason: 'These languages' means C and C++. Section 02 says C++ 1.0 arrived in 1985 and dominated only 'by 2000', so C++ running 'most systems that mattered' by the late 1980s is an overclaim.
judge_fix: "By the late 1980s C ran most systems that mattered and C++ was spreading fast, and many programmers took this as the trade every language must make."

problem: The strip's 'lineage' bullet repeats p9 (write-ahead logging, Chapter 13) and p8 (fsck took hours).
fix: Cut "The lineage" bullet from Fig 4.13's strip.
